h: Romans next door and a town full of history
p: While you're inside the mansion, look out for the picture gallery designed by John Nash, the Regency architect behind Brighton's Royal Pavilion and much of Regent's Park. It's one of the standout rooms in the house and a reminder of just how big the Berwicks were thinking.

Out on the estate, the Mile Walk is a gentle classic, looping through trees and alongside the River Tern. Keep your eyes peeled in the deer park for the herd, and in autumn you might hear the stags during the rut. Wrap up warm on colder days, because the estate is wide and open.

Allow half a day if you want to see the house and do a decent walk, or longer if you've got kids who'll want time in the play areas. Autumn colour and frosty winter mornings make the grounds just as appealing out of season, so it's a good place to come back to.

History fans have a real bonus nearby. A couple of miles away lies Wroxeter Roman City, once one of the largest towns in Roman Britain, cared for by English Heritage. Pairing the two makes a brilliant contrast: Roman ruins in the morning, Regency splendour in the afternoon.

Shrewsbury itself is only a few miles away and well worth an evening wander. The town sits in a loop of the River Severn, packed with timber-framed buildings, steep little alleys locals call shuts, and independent shops. Charles Darwin was born here, Shrewsbury Abbey is famous through the Brother Cadfael stories, and the riverside park known as the Quarry is lovely for a stroll on a summer evening.
